Embodied Experimental Philosophy

Borrow Fire, Then Become Fire · MAIN SEQUENCE 17 / 18

Practice: becoming fire through environment and feedback

Bring works into embodied life; use practice and reflection to revise explanations, boundaries, and aims.

Home · 简体中文

An arrangement looks clear on the page. Someone lives through it, and a small hesitation changes the question. A revised question gives the next arrangement another shape. The world has entered the argument.

Philosophy can give a practice concepts, images, and reasons through which it becomes intelligible. It can also enter the practice it describes. An account of how a person and a model should cooperate can reshape a working environment; the person then encounters the arrangement through perception, attention, effort, action, and other people's responses. Those encounters can reveal something the account had not distinguished.

Embodied experimental philosophy names the proposal developed here: construct a meaningful arrangement, participate in it, and let its consequences inform both its realization and the philosophy guiding it. The bodily life of the person gives the inquiry a concrete situation. Experiment gives a proposed relation a way to meet something beyond its own coherence. Reflection develops what that encounter warrants and what should change next.

Participation and explanation

Participating in a practice and explaining it ask different questions. A reader may understand a theory of attention yet discover through using an interface that its explanations arrive at an exhausting rhythm. Someone else may use the same interface easily while remaining unable to explain why. Experience can disclose a relevant distinction; investigation can examine its conditions and develop an explanation.

Dewey's Reconstruction in Philosophy connects experience with acting and undergoing the consequences of action, and argues for an operative, experimental philosophy [1]. This supplies a philosophical starting point. Here its contemporary development concerns model-supported work: an idea can become a prompt, a role, an interface, or software, giving participation and explanation a common object through which to inform each other.

Embodiment matters because the arrangement is used by someone whose time, attention, perception, and capacity to act have a particular situation. A beautiful explanation that cannot be followed under those conditions may need another expression. A surprising ease of use can suggest an unrecognized relation. Neither observation by itself identifies its mechanism; both can make a useful question available.

The model can carry implementation and investigation while the person understands through the resulting work, contributes experience, and redirects the inquiry. The distributed-practice essay explains how representations and contextual roles connect these contributions. Their division follows the purpose. Learning a particular skill may require exercising it; understanding and using a work can warrant a different division.

Intuition proposes; consequences distinguish

An intuition can recognize a mismatch before a full explanation is available. Perhaps repeated questions interrupt the work; perhaps an autonomous action misses a choice only the person could make. Each perception opens competing interpretations. The problem may involve wording, timing, a missing fact, a tool's behavior, or an inappropriate allocation of responsibility.

Abduction proposes an explanation that would make the observations intelligible. Reasoning unfolds its consequences. A small construction can then make the important difference encounterable. If the hypothesis concerns timing, changing only the wording may leave it unexamined. If it concerns responsibility, a new interface may succeed because it changes who makes a decision. Explicit relations help the experiment discriminate rather than merely produce another impressive output.

Formal reasoning and intuitive inquiry contribute to the same work. A valid derivation establishes a consequence under its premises; experience helps examine whether the premises address the phenomenon. An intuitive proposal can have reasons without being established as the best explanation. Revision can affect either the explanation or the way its consequence was tested.

Two connected loops

A practice loop connects a situated proposal, its realization, participation, and correction. A reflection loop, within its current question and standards, revisits how the activity is understood: which concepts and purposes organize it, what supports a model, what another interpretation would change, and whether the arrangement should be revised. Philosophical argument, engineering investigation, and empirical inquiry can contribute as the question needs. Calling the second loop reflection leaves room for all three without classifying every personal experiment as scientific research. These names organize this proposal, rather than defining every technical account of double-loop learning or second-order cybernetics.

Practice can change an interface after one concrete failure. Reflection can ask whether that failure depended on the task, presentation, or person's circumstances. It may compare cases or construct a more explicit model. Its findings can return to the practical arrangement. Practice also changes as reflection proceeds, so an earlier result has conditions and a history rather than an unlimited guarantee.

The two loops are themselves a chosen arrangement. When inquiry questions that division and the remit or standards of reflection itself, it takes the current pair as its object rather than continuing within those accepted terms. The next section develops this change of scope. Both loops and their relation remain revisable; the pair does not enclose every possible question about the arrangement.

The investigator participates too. An explanation changes what a reader notices; a tool changes what a person can do; asking a question can change the response. The inquiry therefore needs relevant records of its own interventions, not only the results it receives. Describing this involvement helps distinguish a change in the practice from a change in our understanding of it.

“Experimental” here includes philosophical experimentation through making, participation, and reflection. Contemporary experimental philosophy also has a specific empirical research tradition: Knobe and Nichols describe systematic studies of the processes behind philosophical intuitions [2]. Such research can contribute where its methods fit. Trying a personal arrangement and receiving a response constitute a more local achievement.

Reasoning outside the current double-loop arrangement

The reasoning needed here can proceed outside the current double-loop arrangement, taking both loops and their relation as objects. Improving practice under an existing question, or improving reflection under its existing standards, leaves parts of the arrangement accepted. A different question asks why these activities were divided this way, which purposes justify the division, what counts as evidence, and whether the reflection loop's questions and methods should change. Reasoning at this level can revise the reflection loop itself, reconnect it with practice, or replace the arrangement.

A formal or computational system gives an inquiry selected objects, rules, states, and possible transitions. Such selection makes reasoning tractable. Ashby's account of coupling and circular influence explains feedback among parts of a dynamic system [3]; dynamic logic makes actions and changing states objects of formal reasoning [5]. These are resources for understanding work within a selected system. The present proposal also makes that selection, including the reflective arrangement through which it is assessed, available for reconsideration. This further move is the essay's philosophical proposal, rather than a claim established by those technical accounts.

Suppose an assistant maximizes completed outputs, while a reflection loop compares ways of improving that measure. Better scheduling changes practice; a better comparison changes reflection. The whole arrangement may nevertheless keep filling the person's day with work they no longer want. Taking a standpoint outside this pair allows the person and model to question why output count organizes both loops, whether the practice–reflection division serves this life, and what kinds of experience should inform judgment. They can then change the reflection loop's purpose, evidence standards, or relation to practice, as well as the assistant's behavior. The revised arrangement meets the world again through its consequences.

“Outside” is relative to the framework currently being examined. This reasoning still draws on situated experience, language, other representations, and the world. It supplies no position outside every possible framework, and it need not be installed as a fixed third loop that would become another unquestioned enclosure. What matters is keeping the current organization available for judgment and transformation.

Carnap's distinction between questions within a linguistic framework and the practical choice of a framework offers a neighboring resource [4]. Here that comparison helps distinguish inquiry using an arrangement from inquiry that reconsiders the arrangement, including its reflection loop. Connecting this distinction to intervention and consequences is the present proposal; the comparison does not by itself establish how any particular revision will work.

A public work as a concrete experiment

Consider a hypothetical philosophical essay published on the Web from a maintained GitHub source. A reader follows its diagram and finds that a crucial arrow seems to express causation although the text intended analogy. Their correction gives the author and model a specific difference to examine. They revise the relation, its explanation, and the diagram at the source, then check the website's rendered result. If the same misunderstanding shaped an assistant's conduct, they also revise the affected instructions and inspect actual behavior.

This passage joins publication, reception, interpretation, source maintenance, and runtime realization. The Trinity develops their different functions. The published work acquires enough independence to be understood in a way its makers did not predict. The return can revise both expression and practice.

WeChat Moments can offer another encounter when a person chooses to share a work there. Responses from that circle can disclose a reader's question or an unexpected interpretation. They do not constitute a representative sample of society; silence can have several explanations. Their useful contribution is a situated clue that further inquiry may develop. This example proposes no actual posting or obligation to keep monitoring readers.

Finish a version, leave room for return

A coherent version gives something real to encounter. Quick iteration works when each version preserves the relations needed for its purpose, and checks address the uncertainty that could materially change the result. Waiting for a total theory can prevent the very encounters needed to develop it; publishing an unexamined construction can simply spread its mistake. A usable version and proportionate verification connect speed with learning.

Completion and revisability support each other. A work can be finished for its present purpose, then revised when a new question or consequence gives reason. The creation method carries this into working harnesses. The personal-first argument explains why a person's developing understanding and agency orient that work.

The experimental ambition is to give philosophy contact: let reasons become arrangements, let arrangements enter embodied life, and let what happens return as material for understanding. The world contributes to the argument through consequences that neither person nor model can settle by agreement.

Sources and scope

The two-loop organization and examples are this essay's synthesis, not reports of completed experiments or a general demonstration of model-assisted human development.

  1. John Dewey (1920), Reconstruction in Philosophy, especially chapters IV–V. Original text. Acting, undergoing, and operative philosophical inquiry.
  2. Joshua Knobe and Shaun Nichols (2008), An Experimental Philosophy Manifesto, pp.3–14 in Experimental Philosophy. Author-hosted proof. The distinct contemporary empirical tradition; the linked file is an uncorrected proof.
  3. W. Ross Ashby (1956), An Introduction to Cybernetics, chapter 4, especially §4/11. Estate-authorized text. Coupling and feedback within dynamic systems.
  4. Rudolf Carnap (1950), Empiricism, Semantics, and Ontology. Public reprint. Framework-relative inquiry and practical framework adoption, used here as a philosophical comparison.
  5. David Harel, Dexter Kozen, and Jerzy Tiuryn (2000), Dynamic Logic. Author's introduction. Formal reasoning about programs and their effects on states.
